\chapter{Review --- the Whole Preterite}
\label{ch:repaso-preterito}
\hlchaptermodality{204}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give the whole preterite, six people and three families.}

I can give the whole preterite, six people and three families.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[the whole preterite]{Review — the whole preterite}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-repaso-preterito}



\begin{quote}
The past \emph{they} ending for \emph{-ar}? (\textbf{-aron}.) For \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir}? (\textbf{-ieron}.) That is the whole plural, in two syllables each.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say each family's own line, one at a time. There is no table here on purpose — a paradigm is easier to hold as three short chants than as a grid.

\begin{quote}
\emph{-ar}: \textbf{hablé · hablaste · habló · hablamos · hablaron}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{-er}: \textbf{comí · comiste · comió · comimos · comieron}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{-ir}: \textbf{viví · viviste · vivió · vivimos · vivieron}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Two ending sets, not three.} \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} have shared this tense from the first chapter of it, and go on sharing it here.

\textbf{And one person is still missing.} The \emph{vosotros} form — \emph{hablasteis}, \emph{comisteis} — has not been taught, so this is five of the six the present tense gave you. The strong verbs are shorter still: you have \emph{tuve} and \emph{tuvieron}, but not \emph{tuvimos}. Both are owed, and it is better to know that than to think the tense is finished.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two quiet overlaps}]
Worth holding, because neither is a mistake:

\textbf{1. \emph{hablamos} and \emph{vivimos} are each two tenses.} Present and past, identical. Only \emph{comer} keeps them apart — \emph{comemos} against \emph{comimos} — and only because its past borrowed \emph{-imos} from the \emph{-ir} family.

\textbf{2. The strong stems are four words, not a rule.} \emph{Tuv-}, \emph{hic-}, \emph{estuv-}, and \emph{fue-}. Everything else about them is ordinary: they take \emph{-ieron} like any \emph{-er} verb, except \emph{fueron}, which takes nothing at all and just adds \emph{-ron}.

So the only memorising this tense ever asked of you was four stems.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the \emph{ellos} form of \emph{hablar}, \emph{comer}, \emph{vivir}, \emph{tener}, \emph{ser}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many ending sets does the plural need? (\textbf{Two}.) How many stems had to be learned by heart? (\textbf{Four}.) And is the tense finished? (\textbf{Not quite} — \emph{vosotros} is still owed, and so are the strong \emph{nosotros} forms.)
\end{tcolorbox}
